decisions.quote:
Specifically, we revisited Loftus et al.’s (1978) study, focusing on
the 1-day delayed questionnaire condition of Experiment 3, to
provide a contemporary validation of the misinformation effect.
When implementing a GTA-based video of the car-pedestrian
collision and videotaped cowitness narrative in an online setting, we
successfully replicated the original misinformation effect. Misled
participants were more likely to report the incorrect traffic sign
information compared with control participants (i.e., 34% difference
in accuracy between conditions), yielding a moderate effect (Cramer’s
V = 0.37).
decisions.reason: The record is a replication collecting new online data to re-test the postevent misinformation effect from Experiment 3 (1-day delayed condition) of Loftus, Miller, & Burns (1978; DOI: 10.1037/0278-7393.4.1.19). In Study 1 (n = 289), misled participants were significantly less accurate on the binary forced-choice traffic sign recognition test than controls (27.08% vs. 64.55%, chi-square(1) = 28.88, p < .001, Cramer's V = 0.37, BF10 = 824908.67), and in Study 2's incentivized betting-form extension (n = 226) misled participants also allocated significantly more points to the misled item than controls (55.78 vs. 39.53, t(149) = 2.32, p = .011, d = 0.38). (Study 3's reversed-order procedure presented misinformation before the event to test competing memory-trace mechanisms and contrasts with prior reversed-order studies such as Lindsay & Johnson, 1989 and Rantzen & Markham, 1992, not Loftus et al.'s postevent misinformation finding.) The authors state an explicit overall verdict that they 'successfully replicated the original misinformation effect', confirming the shipped outcome 'successful'.

decisions.reason: Shipped row 435 represents Loftus, Miller, & Burns (1978, 10.1037/0278-7393.4.1.19) Experiment 3 (1-day delayed postevent misinformation condition), tested in Studies 1 and 2 and adjudicated in canonical adjudications/f915a8798237e4f0.json. In Study 3 (Reversed Order Study, N=221, pages 11-13; preregistered at https://osf.io/y75c8/), Wiechert et al. (2025) empirically retest the reversed-order misinformation procedure (presenting the cowitness narrative in Session 1, one day before the original accident video and recognition test in Session 2) to adjudicate between single-trace/blocking and activation-based multiple-trace accounts. Study 3 found a nonsignificant, Bayesian-inconclusive difference between misled (58.40%) and control (67.10%) conditions (chi-square(1) = 1.21, p = .272, Cramer's V = 0.09, BF01 = 1.65). The Introduction (page 3) states that the authors replicated the reversed-order procedure, citing Rantzen & Markham (1992, 10.1080/00221309.1992.9921156), and the General Discussion (page 14) contrasts Study 3's null result with both Lindsay & Johnson (1989) and Rantzen & Markham (1992). However, prior v1 review and Luna erred in counting both co-cited papers as separate missing rows from distinct DOIs alone. Primary context 0097 shows that Rantzen & Markham (1992) cites Lindsay & Johnson (1989) in Crossref metadata, but both originals are primary-body and abstract inaccessible. Without primary access to either original's published findings and conditions, actual evidence cannot determine whether Rantzen & Markham (1992) is the single closest replication-chain link or whether Study 3 independently retests one versus both originals.

decisions.reason: Shipped row 435 represents Loftus, Miller, & Burns (1978, 10.1037/0278-7393.4.1.19) Experiment 3 (postevent misinformation), tested in Studies 1 and 2 and adjudicated in canonical adjudications/f915a8798237e4f0.json. In Study 3 (Reversed Order Study, N=221, pages 11-13; preregistered at https://osf.io/y75c8/), Wiechert et al. (2025) empirically retest the reversed-order misinformation procedure (presenting misleading or consistent narrative in Session 1, 24 hours before the original accident video and recognition test in Session 2), observing no significant misinformation effect (58.40% misled vs. 67.10% control; chi-square(1) = 1.21, p = .272, Cramer's V = 0.09, BF01 = 1.65). While the Introduction (page 3) cites Rantzen & Markham (1992) when motivating the reversed-order replication, the General Discussion (page 14) explicitly states that Study 3 contrasts previous studies using the reversed-order methodology, naming both Lindsay & Johnson (1989, 10.3758/BF03329912) and Rantzen & Markham (1992). Prior v1 review and Luna treated both co-cited papers as separate missing rows based on distinct DOIs alone. In primary context 0097, Crossref reference metadata confirms that Rantzen & Markham (1992) cites Lindsay & Johnson (1989), indicating a direct citation chain, but neither 1989 nor 1992 primary text or abstract is accessible. Because actual evidence cannot establish the exact published reversed-order findings/conditions in Lindsay & Johnson (1989) versus Rantzen & Markham (1992) or whether 1992 supersedes 1989 as the single closest replication-chain link for the same finding, Target 2 is undeterminable.
